frameworks.name: Seven-Step Lead Magnet Creation Framework
frameworks.definition: A sequential checklist for designing lead magnets: (1) define the problem and audience, (2) choose how to solve it, (3) choose delivery mechanism, (4) package/name it, (5) make it fast and easy to consume, (6) make it genuinely excellent, (7) make the next step easy and clear.

frameworks.name: Complete Solution to Narrow Problem
frameworks.definition: A lead magnet is a fully complete solution to one narrowly defined micro-step problem within the customer journey, not a partial solution gated behind a paywall; solving it completely opens the prospect to the next sequential problem, which becomes the paid offer.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the primary reason businesses do not generate enough revenue is insufficient lead volume, and the primary reason for insufficient leads is not giving away enough high-quality free value (lead magnets) up front.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Free value delivered before purchase creates a prediction of future value in the prospect's mind, causing them to trust and buy; without that prediction, the prospect has no evidence to act on.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a lead magnet must be a complete solution to a narrowly defined problem, not a partial solution designed to force a purchase; giving partial work destroys trust and inverts the purpose of the lead magnet.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: A partial solution signals to the prospect that the business withholds value, reducing the prediction of future value and therefore reducing willingness to buy.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi contends that a properly designed lead magnet lowers the total cost to acquire a customer even when the lead magnet itself costs money to deliver, because higher trial take-up rates from a discounted or free front-end offer convert a larger downstream paying cohort.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service or product business with a back-end paid offer
Lead magnet is genuinely good and delivers complete value
claims.mechanism: Lower perceived risk of the front-end offer attracts a larger prospect pool; even a fraction converting to the core offer at full price produces higher total revenue than a smaller high-barrier pool closing at the same rate.

numbers.axis: leads-to-revenue comparison: direct offer ($100) vs. discounted lead magnet ($10) approach, using a 100-person prospect pool

anchors.takers: ~20 people; 30% convert to $100 back-end = 6 customers = $600 revenue plus $200 in lead magnet cost net positive

bounded_by: Only holds when the lead magnet quality is high enough to build trust; sucky lead magnets produce negative word of mouth and harm back-end conversion

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that big business owners think long-term, accepting calculated up-front costs on lead magnets because they know the back-end LTV justifies the front-end investment; small business owners avoid those costs and therefore underperform on lead generation.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Businesses with a proven back-end offer whose LTV exceeds lead magnet delivery cost
claims.mechanism: Long-horizon operators use the lead magnet delivery cost as a customer acquisition investment rather than a pure expense, compressing CAC relative to businesses that offer nothing up front.
bounded_by: Requires a back-end offer with positive LTV to justify front-end cost

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that a low-quality (sucky) lead magnet actively harms revenue by producing negative word-of-mouth, causing non-buyers to discourage others who would otherwise have purchased.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Lead magnet reaches the broader marketplace through word of mouth
claims.mechanism: Prospects who consume a weak lead magnet form a negative prediction of future value; when asked about the creator by peers, they report the quality negatively, suppressing purchase intent in otherwise qualified buyers.

numbers.axis: marketplace behavior after consuming a low-quality lead magnet

anchors.outcome: Does not buy (99% only consume and do not convert)
Warned away by negative report from the non-buyer

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that if a lead magnet does not generate voluntary referrals from people who consume it, the lead magnet has failed its purpose.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Lead magnet is intended to grow top-of-funnel audience organically
claims.mechanism: Only genuinely valuable free content creates the surplus value gap that motivates unprompted sharing; sharing compounds reach at zero marginal cost.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that the packaging and naming of a lead magnet is the single most important step in the creation process, because it is the first and often only variable a prospect evaluates before deciding whether to consume the offer.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: A prospect cannot evaluate the quality of the content until after they opt in; the name and packaging is the proxy they use for that evaluation, making it the primary conversion lever before consumption.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that making a lead magnet available in multiple consumption formats (audio, written, hardback, digital, video) can double or triple consumption rates with minimal incremental effort relative to the original creation investment.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Audiences have heterogeneous learning preferences; a single format excludes the segments that prefer other formats, so format expansion captures proportionally more of the same audience.

numbers.axis: consumption split by format for $100 Million Offers (~350,000 copies sold as of recording)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that making the call-to-action (CTA) clear rather than clever multiplies response rates, because clarity removes friction at the decision moment when a prospect is ready to take the next step.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: A clever CTA requires the prospect to interpret what to do next; interpretive friction causes drop-off. A concrete, specific instruction (e.g., go to amazon, search my name) removes the interpretation step and converts intent into action.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that giving away free physical work or services (that incur real cost) is perceived by the marketplace at a significantly higher value percentage than free information assets like PDFs or video series, and therefore attracts more prospects.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Marketplace has been exposed to many free information products (PDFs, video series) and has discounted their perceived value
claims.mechanism: Perceived value of a lead magnet is a function of its scarcity and the effort/cost signal it sends; physical or service-based free work signals higher cost and effort, elevating perceived value above commodity information products.
bounded_by: Requires the delivered work to be genuinely high quality; low-quality service work triggers the same negative word-of-mouth as low-quality information products

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a business solving a sequence of customer problems can structure the first one or two steps as a free lead magnet and charge for the third step, because completing the free steps naturally exposes the customer to the next problem and makes them the most likely buyer of its solution.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Multi-step problem where each step naturally leads to the next
Business has a paid offer addressing a downstream problem in the sequence
claims.mechanism: Solving early steps establishes trust and demonstrated competence; the customer's experience of success at step one/two primes them to want the next solution from the same provider rather than seeking a competitor.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi contends that the free offer's quality should exceed competitors' paid offers; only when the free lead magnet outperforms what others charge for does the business become effectively unstoppable in market competition.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business must have sufficient skill or resources to deliver at that quality level on the front end
claims.mechanism: A free offer that exceeds others' paid alternatives eliminates the prospect's rational basis for choosing a competitor; the trust gap is so large that competitive switching becomes irrational.
bounded_by: Requires the business to have or develop the skill depth to deliver competitor-grade quality for free

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that the choice of delivery mechanism (information, service, or physical product) for a lead magnet should be decided by which mechanism is perceived as highest value by the prospect and which maximizes take-up rate and conversion to the core offer, not by what is cheapest or easiest for the business.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

examples.text: Alex Hormozi illustrates the lead magnet math using a massage business. If you approach 100 people with a $100 massage offer, roughly 1 person says yes. If instead you offer a $10 trial massage to the same 100 people, roughly 20 say yes. Of those 20, about 30% (6 people) later buy the full-price massage package. The $10 trial cost the business roughly $10 in delivery cost per trial, so the lead magnet breaks even or costs a small loss per trial. But converting 6 customers worth ~$2,000 each from a ~$200 lead magnet investment produces dramatically better economics than acquiring 1 customer at $100 direct. The massage subscription or massage packages are the core offer; the $10 trial is the lead magnet.

Hormozi describes how a weight-loss business can structure sequential lead magnets that each solve one narrowly defined micro-problem in the customer journey. Step one: a preloaded Instacart grocery list segmented by gender and weight category, which is one-time work reusable across hundreds of prospect types. Step two: a guide on how to clean and prep all purchased food in under 60 minutes. Step three: how to store and portion it for on-the-go use. Each step, once complete, exposes the customer to the next problem they have not yet solved, making them warm and receptive to the next offer in sequence. The eventual paid offer addresses a downstream problem (e.g., accountability or macro tracking) that naturally follows the free sequence.

Hormozi recounts a book cover testing process to illustrate how naming and packaging determine lead magnet performance. He tested multiple titles in head-to-head A/B fashion: '$100 Million Advertising' vs. '$100 Million Promotions' — Advertising won 69% to 31%. Then 'Advertising' vs. '$100 Million Leads' — Leads won 58% to 42%. Then '$100 Million Leads' vs. '$100 Million Marketing' — Leads won again. Only the title and packaging were tested; no content changed. He also cites an external example: a dating book that tanked on launch but went on to sell over 10 million copies after only the cover and headline were changed — nothing inside the book was altered.

Hormozi uses a house-painting business to illustrate how a multi-step service creates lead magnet opportunities. A full house paint job involves many micro-steps: sizing the house, giving an estimate, the design component, a 3D visualization of the final result, and then the actual painting. A painter could offer the 3D visualization step as a deeply discounted or free lead magnet — doing such a good job that the prospect's trust increases, they have one foot in the door, and they naturally want the same business to handle the next steps.

practices.text: Define the problem you want to solve and who you want to solve it for before building any lead magnet; specificity of avatar changes naming, packaging, marketing, and delivery approach.
Make the call-to-action in any lead magnet or content clear and direct rather than clever; give multiple explicit pathways (URL, phone, QR code) that match different audience preferences.
Put 100 hours of effort into a lead magnet if you have never invested more than 10 hours in one; the quality gap between creators is almost entirely an effort gap, not a talent gap.
Test lead magnet names and packaging (title, sub-headline, image) before finalizing; run head-to-head tests and let data pick the winner rather than relying on internal preference.
Map the complete before-during-after journey of your customer before designing a lead magnet; identify each micro-problem, then select the most painful early micro-problem to solve for free.
